content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler peas, Stage 2 are gently cooked, lightly mashed pea purees designed for children aged 8 to 12 months. The puree is made from selected green peas, without added sugar, salt, or artificial flavors. Its texture supports the development of self‑feeding skills.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peas are one of the first vegetables introduced to infants because of their mild flavor and soft texture.
Stage 2 puree contains small soft pieces to help develop chewing abilities.
Peas are a good source of plant protein, supporting growth and tissue development.
Only whole peas are used, with no added starches or thickeners.
Pea purees are often combined with other vegetables, but this version keeps the pure pea taste.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peas provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle and organ growth.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and regular bowel movements.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Peas contain folate, thiamine, and vitamin B6, important for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: They supply iron, magnesium, and phosphorus, which aid bone development and blood formation.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: No added salt makes the product safe for infants' kidneys.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some children may be allergic to peas; introduce the product under supervision.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Although Stage 2 contains small soft pieces, they should be offered only with adult supervision.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; a varied diet helps mitigate this.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the puree warm (not hot) in a baby bowl. For a thinner consistency, add a little breast milk, formula, or vegetable broth. It can be mixed with soft pieces of potato or carrot for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened package in a cool, dry place. Once opened, store in the refrigerator and use within 3 days. Unused portions can be frozen in an airtight container for up to 1 month. Reheat thoroughly and stir before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Beef, sandwich steak (651) is a thin cut of meat taken from the tenderloin or chuck of a cow. It has a mild flavor, moderate fat content, and cooks quickly, making it ideal for hot sandwiches, burgers, and fast‑cook dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sandwich steaks are usually sliced 1–1.5 cm thick to ensure rapid cooking.
They are a staple in fast‑food outlets because they stay juicy when cooked fast.
Beef provides all essential amino acids, making it a complete protein source.
Traditionally these steaks are grilled or pan‑seared with a little oil.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The steak supplies high‑quality protein needed for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It provides vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin that support energy metabolism.

items.title: Zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals aid immune function and protect against oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Suitable for low‑carb diets as it contains virtually no sugars.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Excessive intake may raise cholesterol levels; choose lean cuts when possible.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor pathogens; cook to an internal temperature of at least 71 °C.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Rare, but some individuals may have an allergic reaction to beef.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Large amounts can exacerbate gout symptoms.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Quickly sear the sandwich steak on high heat for 1–2 minutes per side, then slice thinly. Use it in hot sandwiches, burger patties, salads, or serve with barbecue sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0–4 °C in an airtight container for 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in a bag at –18 °C, where it remains good for up to 6 months. Thaw in the fridge before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Meringues are light, airy desserts made from whipped egg whites and sugar. Sometimes starch, lemon juice, or flavorings are added. After baking they become crisp on the outside and tender inside.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Meringues originated in France in the 17th century and quickly spread across Europe.
The name “meringue” is linked to Swiss confectioner Joseph Meringue, who is said to have created them in 1692.
There are several types: French (whipped whites and sugar only), Swiss (sugar melted with whites), and Italian (hot sugar syrup poured into whipped whites).
Meringues are often used as the base for Pavlova and Baked Alaska desserts.
When properly baked, meringues can be stored for several weeks in a dry place.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Meringues contain virtually no fat, making them a light dessert when eaten in moderation.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Egg whites provide a modest amount of high‑quality protein.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Traditional meringues are naturally gluten‑free, suitable for gluten‑free diets.

items.title: Contains vitamin B2
items.content: Egg whites contain riboflavin (vitamin B2), important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Calorie‑friendly with fruit toppings
items.content: Serving meringues with berries or fruit sauce adds vitamins and fiber without greatly increasing calories.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Meringues contain egg whites, which can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The large amount of sugar makes meringues calorie‑dense and can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: If made from raw eggs without sufficient heat treatment, there is a risk of salmonella.

items.title: Fragility
items.content: Meringues crumble easily, posing a choking hazard for young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Meringues can be enjoyed on their own, used as cake decorations, served with berry sauce, ice cream, or fresh fruit. They can also be crushed and folded into mousses or creams for a light texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store finished meringues in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Properly stored they stay crisp for 2–3 weeks. If they become soft, they can be re‑dried in a low‑temperature oven.

content.title: About
content.content: Whole wheat tortilla is a thin, flexible flatbread made from whole‑grain wheat flour, water, salt, and sometimes a small amount of vegetable oil. It has a mild nutty aroma, a sturdy texture, and a higher fiber content than white flour tortillas.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tortillas originated in Mexico over 3,000 years ago and were originally made from corn; the whole‑wheat version became popular in the United States in the 1970s.
Whole‑grain flour retains the bran and germ, making the tortilla more nutritious than its white counterpart.
Tortillas freeze well and can be reheated in a microwave or on a skillet without losing quality.
In many cuisines they replace bread or flatbreads as a wrap for fillings.
Some whole‑wheat tortillas are labeled “gluten‑free” only when made with alternative grains; standard wheat tortillas contain gluten.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain flour provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting digestive health and promoting satiety.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: The tortilla delivers slow‑releasing glucose, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole wheat supplies thiamine, niacin, and folate, essential for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Iron, magnesium, and zinc in the tortilla contribute to metabolic processes and immune support.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many baked goods, whole‑wheat tortillas contain minimal fat when no extra oil is added.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: People with wheat allergy or celiac disease should avoid whole‑wheat tortillas.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some brands add salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Whole‑wheat tortillas contain gluten and are not suitable for gluten‑free diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use tortillas as the base for burritos, tacos, wraps, and sandwiches. Warm them on a dry skillet for a crisp edge or microwave briefly for flexibility. They pair well with vegetables, beans, lean proteins, cheese, and sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep tortillas in an airtight bag in the refrigerator for up to 7 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a separate bag; they can be reheated directly from frozen without losing pliability.
